Replying to @naomi when pricing my pieces I consider time spent making/decorating/signing/waxing/glazing/sanding/lustering/firing/invetorying. I have done time studies to help gauge the time I spend on making the pieces. I also consider materials used. I apply gold luster to almost every piece and it’s expensive and requires an additional firing which is also another expense. I also consider experience. I have been working with clay for 14 years now so I consider all of those years of working to this point in my pieces value as well. Pricing is hard! Placing a value on your art is uncomfortable. I’m just happy to be here and I’m doing my best with the knowledge I have gained so far on this journey. I don’t think there is a right answer that will work for everyone, I’m just trying to do what feels right to me! Thank you for reading! 💗💗💗💗 #wheelthrown #ceramics #sliptrailing #potterytiktok #porcelain

videos.caption: I have a bit of an exaggerated skirt on this piece so I can show you a couple techniques for removing the skirt from the base of your cylinder. Removing it twice requires a bit of extra clay. In addition new potters who have not yet learned to bring clay up their piece frequently find that there is quite a bit to remove at the end of throwing their piece so this is a reflection of what a beginner might have on the wheel after working hard to bring clay up into the wall. It’s such a common groan from students at Twisted Clay when I tell them to cut their skirt away. They are so worried about ruining the pot as it can be tricky to get your head around, but once you do, you won’t want to skip this step ever again. Not a member of my online studio yet? Throwing a Donut on the Wheel Center your clay and compress it into a wide, flat puck. Poke through the center down to the wheel head and slowly stretch it open to create the donut hole. Split the ring 50/50—leave a base slightly thicker than your future walls. Pull up the inner wall first, then the outer wall. Join the walls together. It doesn’t matter which one overlaps—adjust based on how the clay moves. Before joining, I thin out the edges to avoid a step at the seam. Important! Remove any slip and excess water from the seam—otherwise, it will crack during drying or firing. Once the walls are joined, the trapped air inside acts as a support structure, allowing you to refine the shape and compress the seam. Trim the excess clay inside and out, and your donut is ready! Follow me for more wheel-throwing tips! … … #ceramics #potteryvideos #pottery #fyp #usa
